title: Universities are becoming more efficient but less reflective
summary: Alaa Garad argues the sector's crisis is really about a failure to learn about itself and sets out what universities would need to do to fix that
full_text:
In 1997, Peter Drucker made a remark that felt provocative at the time but increasingly sounds like an observation rather than a prediction: “Universities won’t survive…the future is outside the traditional campus.”

What he was pointing to was not the end of learning, but the slow unravelling of a model that had become overly tied to place, structure, and habit.

Around the same time, Bill Readings, in The University in Ruins, argued that universities were losing their cultural and philosophical centre, held together instead by systems, procedures, and an unexamined pursuit of “excellence.”

Ronald Barnett later offered a more measured warning: universities may not disappear, but without serious reimagining, they risk becoming increasingly irrelevant to the world they claim to serve.

These were not attacks on universities. They were acts of care.

Today, particularly in the UK, higher education finds itself under extraordinary pressure, financially, politically, and socially. Universities are expected to educate, to lead learning, to drive innovation, to support local economies, and to prepare graduates for an uncertain future. And yet, many institutions appear to struggle with learning about themselves.

I write this not as an external critic, but as someone who has been part of the system for most of his life – as a student, researcher, academic, external examiner, and senior executive, across 11 universities. What continues to strike me is not a lack of intelligence or commitment, but a shared institutional stiffness. There is an unspoken consensus across the sector: bureaucracy has become heavy, and change has become difficult.

As a quality and organisational learning professional, I fully appreciate the importance of governance, academic integrity, and reputational protection. These matter. But when governance becomes primarily about avoiding risk rather than enabling learning, something vital is lost.

Universities begin to operate on autopilot, efficient perhaps, but no longer reflective.

The customer is sometimes right

One example illustrates this tension clearly.

Many senior leaders resist referring to students as “customers,” fearing a slide into crude marketisation. The concern is understandable. But denying the term does not remove the reality that students invest significant time, money, and trust in their institutions. The real question is not whether students are customers, but whether universities are genuinely listening to them.

Similarly, management tools such as balanced scorecards or international standards are often dismissed as “commercial” and therefore unsuitable for academia. But universities are organisations operating in a competitive environment. The issue is not the tools themselves, it’s how thoughtfully they are used.

When designed around purpose rather than control, such tools can support learning rather than undermine it. The current financial crisis facing UK universities has further exposed a deeper mindset issue. Faced with pressure, many institutions have turned first to cost-cutting and sometimes in ways that feel symbolically small but culturally significant.

Reducing student support or staff wellbeing may balance a spreadsheet, but it rarely builds trust or long-term resilience. Growth, diversification, and innovation are harder conversations, but they are ultimately the more responsible ones.

If universities are serious about learning, then their governance systems must also learn. That means listening to feedback, benchmarking beyond the sector, and ensuring that leadership accountability is about capability and contribution, not tenure.

It also means moving beyond ceremonial governance, where decisions are routinely approved but rarely challenged.

Constructive foot forward

So what might a constructive way forward look like?

It begins by recognising that the current crisis is not simply a funding problem, but a learning problem.

Many universities are struggling not because they lack expertise, but because their systems are poorly designed to learn, adapt, and reconfigure themselves in response to change.

This is where the concept of the Learning‑Driven Organisation (LDO), developed by Garad and Gold, becomes particularly relevant. The LDO reframes learning not as a support activity or cultural aspiration, but as the primary strategic engine through which organisations achieve innovation, foresight, and sustainable excellence.

In this view, learning is not something universities do, it’s how they survive.

UK universities already excel at disciplinary and individual learning. What they often lack, however, is enterprise-level organisational learning – the capacity to understand themselves as complex systems.

Becoming truly learning-driven requires institutions to embed learning explicitly within strategy, governance, and performance management, rather than assuming it will emerge organically from academic activity.

This involves articulating a shared institutional learning vision, aligned with public purpose, financial sustainability, and societal impact. It also requires governing bodies and executive teams to treat learning as a board-level responsibility, supported by structured reflection, feedback loops, and evidence-based decision-making.

Building a learning ecosystem

In times of crisis, universities often respond with isolated measures: restructures, new programmes, or efficiency drives.

By contrast, learning-focused institutions take a broader approach. They cultivate coherent learning ecosystems where people, processes, technology, and partnerships continuously reinforce one another, creating sustainable and mutually supportive growth.

The Organisational Learning Standard (OLS), which builds on the LDO model, provides a practical framework for doing this. It integrates culture, policies, infrastructure, innovation, people, measurement, and future readiness into a single learning system.

For universities, this means aligning academic development, professional services learning, student feedback, digital capability, and external partnerships into a shared architecture, rather than treating them as separate domains.

The financial pressures facing UK universities have pushed many institutions toward short-term cost-cutting that risks undermining long‑term capability. A learning‑driven approach reframes productivity not as “doing more with less,” but as learning how to create more value with what already exists.

This includes redesigning academic work to focus on learning impact rather than volume, using digital and AI-enabled tools to enhance feedback and assessment, and enabling cross-functional collaboration that reduces duplication and institutional silos.

Productivity, in this sense, becomes an outcome of better learning design, not austerity.

Embedding crystal ball thinking

One of the most damaging aspects of the current crisis is how many universities were surprised by it.

Learning‑driven institutions institutionalise foresight – the structured exploration of future scenarios – as a normal part of strategic learning.

Horizon scanning, scenario planning, and futures literacy enable universities to anticipate shifts in demographics, regulation, technology, and labour markets, and to adapt their learning portfolios and business models before crises emerge. Foresight, in the LDO and OLS frameworks, is not an add-on but a natural extension of learning maturity.

Let’s get (un)comfortable

Finally, universities must overcome their discomfort with measurement.

Avoiding metrics does not protect academic values, it obscures learning. Learning‑driven institutions measure not only financial results, but learning performance, innovation outcomes, staff engagement, student experience, and societal contribution.

Crucially, measurement should serve learning, not control. Balanced scorecards, learning indicators, and feedback systems become tools for reflection and improvement – helping universities understand what is working, what is not, and why.

Universities still matter deeply. But caring about their future requires honesty about their present. The choice is not between tradition and change, it’s between reflection and drift.

In an era of profound uncertainty, the most sustainable university will not be the largest or the most prestigious, but the one that learns fastest and most honestly. And universities, of all institutions, should understand the value of learning.

For those attending this year’s party conferences, join HEPI for our 2026 Party Conference ringe events, at the Labour Party Conference on Monday 28 September in Liverpool and the Conservative Party Conference on Monday 5 October in Birmingham.

This blog was kindly authored by Dr John Cater, Vice-Chancellor, Edge Hill University (1993-2025), current chair of the Unite Foundation.

The escalator clanks its way skywards from the bowels of the underground. Eyes averted and heads turned to the wall, each passing A3 poster advertising a provider of higher education. Emerging at ground level, beneath rotating neon signs – January starts, flexible learning – the message is reaffirmed by the billboard posters and the rear panel of a passing red bus.

Surfaced, internet signal regained, the smartphone pings, a course here, a programme there…

But, opening the pages of the morning’s broadsheet, a counter message. The newspaper incessantly queries the value of higher education, debunking its worth, focussing on ‘debt’, championing apprenticeships. And, under attack, higher education feels under-appreciated, seems unsure of how to respond.

One hopes that no civilised society would argue that it should be less educated, less skilled, but the implicit, and increasingly explicit, message, “don’t go”, is writ large in the media and in political newspeak. For now, universities – or at least a proportion of them – remain at the top of the perceptual hierarchy when it comes to the choices of many (and their families and peers) at the age of eighteen, as is evidenced by the stable (and, based on applicant statistics, arguably increasing) proportion of the age cohort submitting their UCAS form. But, notwithstanding the absence (to date) of mass take-up of apprenticeships or T-levels, the siren sounds grow louder. And, with 16% fewer eighteen-year-olds in the 2030s and the likelihood of increased State control of in-migration, the need for higher education to sustain and increase its appeal to the present populace, the politicians and the press, is of paramount importance if the sector is to prosper or, indeed, if some providers are to survive.

Part of securing this sustenance can be driven by product and mode, but there is much to be gained in changing perception, and, in particular, repeatedly challenging the false dichotomy between ‘academic’ learning and skills, between universities and further education colleges and between universities and the labour market. The most important skills in securing initial employment are generic skills and attributes, developed and delivered at least equally well in a university context. Further, in most universities, specific job skills and programmes leading to professional accreditation – medicine, nursing, teaching and much more – constitute a significant part of the portfolio.

But how universities present themselves matters too. Emerging from the Underground, bombarded by advertising, there is a danger that the message was one of desperation, not aspiration. And this is reinforced by the sector’s use of social media. All too often universities pour money into Google Adwords, but with very low click through rates and extremely short ‘dwell’ times, without asking themselves whether this should be the principal vehicle through which we are seeking to persuade an individual to make one of life’s more important decisions, educatively, personally, financially.

For this author, whilst a necessary part of a marketing strategy, the predominant use of social media is a measure of the laziness of an institution’s approach to recruitment. Clicked and swiped in a fraction of a second, social media is consumed, if it is consumed at all, by a single individual. Swamped by other uses and other users, and, doubtless, by more engaging content, its impact is clearly waning, and at pace. And, is this really the place to determine the next three years and beyond? The place to make one of the most significant financial decisions of an entire working life (a commitment to pay an additional nine percent income tax once above the threshold for up to four decades)?

So what is the alternative? Brand awareness matters, and that can be achieved by advertising, ideally through a wide range of media – using differing mediums (see, hear, read), and sufficient frequencies (see, recognise, engage). But, for real impact, create conversations. A communication with one person is unlikely to extend beyond that person. If two people knowingly receive the same communication, there are two possible engagements (A>B, B<A); if three, (A>B, A>C, B>C, C>B, C>A, B>A), six; if four, twelve. And recognise the importance of tailoring and sharing communications with stakeholders other than potential applicants – peers and tutors, parents and, increasingly, grandparents.

But building a reputable brand requires more than an ad-word, a billboard or the back of a bus. Effective marketing is hard work, and it requires personal contact and relationship-building. It is two decades since the first iteration of Aim Higher drew to a close, but what underpinned it, universities working coherently and consistently with schools (from key stages 1 and 2 onwards) and colleges, with careers advisers, with stakeholders and communities, was of real value. Notwithstanding workload pressures and resource constraints, there is no greater priority. The bedrock of financial stability and job security comes from successful recruitment and retention, and ensuring the quality of the student experience, of which more in a follow-up blog.

title: ‘Internal exclusion’ of England secondary school students almost triples in three years
summary:
Exclusive: new data shows poorer pupils and those with Send are disproportionately affected by the measure

The proportion of secondary school students in England removed from class and placed in “internal exclusion” as a disciplinary measure has almost trebled in three years, according to new data.

The data shows the proportion of secondary pupils removed from normal lessons went up from 5% in the 2022/2023 academic year to 13% in 2025/26 – a 160% increase.

Continue reading...
full_text:
The proportion of secondary school students in England removed from class and placed in “internal exclusion” as a disciplinary measure has almost trebled in three years, according to new data.

The data shows the proportion of secondary pupils removed from normal lessons went up from 5% in the 2022/2023 academic year to 13% in 2025/26 – a 160% increase.

Poorer children are disproportionately affected, with more than one in five (22%) disadvantaged youngsters taken out of lessons at least once in 2025/26, up from 8% three years ago – a 175% increase, according to analysis of the data. The figure was one in ten (10%) for non-disadvantaged pupils.

Children with special educational needs and disabilities (Send) are also overrepresented, with 18% of students with an education, health and care plan removed from class at least once in 2025/26.

Critics say that putting pupils into internal exclusion – which varies between schools but is sometimes described as an “isolation room” – can damage mental wellbeing and result in lost learning. Others say it is an effective tool in behaviour management.

The data was collected and analysed by Arbor, a management information system used by 13,000 schools across England, and shared exclusively with the Guardian.

Fewer than 1% of primary pupils were internally excluded at least once in a year. In 2025/6 the number of under-11s affected was almost 5,000, though the real figure is likely to be significantly higher, as Arbor does not have data for every school.

Unlike permanent exclusions and fixed term suspensions, when pupils are sent home, internal exclusions require children to remain on site and they are returned to their class at the end of the exclusion. While the government collects data on exclusions and suspensions, it does not for internal exclusions.

Arbor’s CEO and co-founder, James Weatherill, said: “Schools clearly need effective ways to respond when behaviour disrupts learning, and we know from schools that internal exclusion can be an important alternative to sending a pupil home. But the scale of this increase, particularly among disadvantaged pupils, should prompt us to look more closely at what is driving it.”

The rise in internal exclusions, as recorded by Arbor’s live national data, comes at a time when official figures published by the Department for Education (DfE) showed formal suspensions and exclusions fell last year.

“We cannot tell from these figures whether one is replacing the other, but the divergence underlines why government needs a more complete picture of how many pupils are being removed from their normal lessons, for how long, and with what consequences,” said Weatherill.

Pepe Di’Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said: “Internal exclusions are never used lightly but only after other avenues have been exhausted. They are a step short of an external exclusion and are designed to keep the student in school with appropriate learning support.”

Lily Wielar, researcher at the Education Policy Institute, said: “Classroom removal has become a deeply embedded feature of behaviour management in England’s secondary schools.

“We urgently need to know more about how classroom removal is being used, and to ensure that removed pupils have the same legal protections and transparency that apply elsewhere.”

Tom Bennett, a leading expert in behaviour management, said: “Internal exclusions are, of course, a form of inclusion. A way to show students who disrupt the learning or safety of others that their actions have consequences, but in a way that means they aren’t simply sitting at home doing nothing, or worse, exposed to unsupportive environments.

“It means that learning can be delivered on site, and in an environment where staff ratios are higher, work can be done on their social skills and behaviour, but away from the students whose learning and safety has been damaged – because they matter too.”

Dame Rachel de Souza, children’s commissioner for England, said: “Excluding a child from the classroom can be necessary to protect other children, but every child should be supported to learn alongside their peers. Where that isn’t possible, children should still be receiving a high-quality education as part of internal exclusion – and I’m concerned that might not always be the case.”

The DfE has been contacted for comment.

title: Undocumented Students Grapple With Loss of In-State Tuition
summary:
Undocumented Students Grapple With Loss of In-State Tuition
Olivia.sanchez Wed, 09/02/2026 - 03:00 AM

Students face uncertainty, large tuition bills and emotional distress when policy changes strip them of access to in-state tuition prices.

Byline(s)
Olivia Sanchez
full_text:
Growing up in South Texas, Kendra always dreamed of becoming a doctor or a nurse. When she graduated from high school and enrolled at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, she said she spent her entire first year trying to connect with her professors and asking for opportunities to shadow clinicians.

Kendra, now 21, was born in Mexico and came to the United States with her parents when she was 9. (Kendra asked to be identified by her first name only.) She knew that being in the country without authorization would make it difficult for her to land the clinical placements necessary for most medical education programs—but it didn’t stop her from trying.

Halfway through her freshman year, President Donald Trump took office for the second time. Kendra said her family feared immigration enforcement raids and warned her not to go anywhere she didn’t need to go. She did her best not to let it distract her from her studies. But she said she was shocked when she learned last summer that the Texas Dream Act was in jeopardy.

The law, which made undocumented students eligible to pay in-state tuition rates, was the only reason Kendra could afford to go to college. Without it, she wouldn’t be able to stay at UTRGV. “That can’t happen,” she said.

But it did. In June 2025, the Department of Justice sued the state, arguing the law discriminated against U.S. citizens in other states. Texas quickly capitulated, and a district judge blocked the law. An appeals court later upheld the ruling.

Kendra was forced to reassess everything.

“You go from feeling like you’re worth it to feeling like complete crap,” Kendra said. “It doesn’t only affect the money.”

Kendra is one of more than 120,000 undocumented college students who have lost access to in-state tuition because of Department of Justice lawsuits in Texas, as well as Oklahoma, Nebraska, Kentucky and Illinois.

Since then, as part of the Trump administration’s wide-ranging anti-immigration campaign, the DOJ has filed lawsuits against similar policies in 20 other states, putting more than 218,000 more undocumented students at risk of losing their in-state tuition eligibility, according to data from the Higher Education Immigration Portal.

The DOJ’s lawsuits argue that offering in-state tuition to undocumented students gives them an unfair advantage over U.S. citizen students from other states, and incentivizes illegal immigration.

But advocates say such policies offer a pathway for young people who want to study and get good jobs so they can contribute to their communities. If they have to pay out-of-state tuition prices, a college education can quickly become out of reach.

Miriam Feldblum, president and CEO of the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, said maintaining the policies is a matter of fairness and consistency; before Trump took office for the second time, 25 states and Washington, D.C., allowed undocumented students to pay in-state tuition rates.

“The administration is targeting higher education access and affordability for undocumented students in ways that make no economic, educational or national sense,” Feldblum said. “We should use all the tools in our toolbox to strengthen our states’ economies.”

Just because in-state tuition has been struck down in some states doesn’t necessarily mean it won’t survive elsewhere, Feldblum said. The policies are all a little different, which can work to their advantage, she said.

“We don’t know yet what is going to happen with all the lawsuits,” she said. “The courts can really reach different conclusions based on the specific laws and the questions presented.”

‘It’s Just Not Fair’

The experience of students like Kendra offers a glimpse into how disruptive the policy change can be for noncitizen students, many of whom were brought to the U.S. as children.

After the Texas policy was struck down, Kendra took several months off from school and even briefly considered going back to Mexico, where she thought she might have more educational and career opportunities. Eventually, she decided to stay in the U.S. and transfer to South Texas College, where her scholarship from TheDream.US covers much more than it would have at the four-year university. Instead of premed, she’s now pursuing an associate degree in child development.

Although she’s at a new school, Kendra said she takes a bus to the UTRGV campus to study with her friends who are still students there. She asks them to tell her what they’re learning in their classes so that if she ever goes back, she won’t be far behind, she said.

Susan Collins, chief of staff and government affairs at TheDream.US, which offers scholarships to undocumented students, said that after the Texas Dream Act was struck down, her organization scrambled to help students like Kendra transfer to other colleges. “But at the end of the day, it’s not a solution,” she said.

“The ongoing fight over the tuition-equity question just underscores the need for a permanent federal solution that finally puts Dreamers on a path to citizenship and full inclusion,” Collins said.

Not all students who lost access to in-state tuition have transferred. Some, including 22-year-old Beth, fought hard to stay.

Beth was about to start her senior year as a strategic communications major at the University of Houston when she learned the Texas Dream Act was ending. She said she cried almost every day as she tried to figure out what she had to do to get the credits she needed to graduate.

“You don’t understand, I can’t transfer to a different university,” said Beth, a pseudonym. “All the things that I’ve built at the University of Houston, all my leadership, all my volunteer hours, all my connections—I can’t just let them go.”

Beth, who was brought to the United States when she was just a year old, said she took on work on campus, did freelance design work and borrowed money from her mother to pay her tuition bill, which went from roughly $6,000 to $14,000 per semester.

“It’s just very frustrating because … I don’t drink. I don’t do drugs. I don’t get in fights. I don’t do anything wrong. I’m always there helping out people,” Beth said. “It’s just not fair.”

Despite the financial burden, extra work and added stress brought on by the policy change, she managed to graduate on time in May.

Others may not be so fortunate.

Wil Del Pilar, senior vice president at EdTrust, a research and advocacy nonprofit, said the DOJ lawsuits are creating confusion for undocumented students and their families across the country—not only in the states where the policies have changed.

“I think it’s incredibly shortsighted to limit access to education and training to a group that may be your next group of inventors or they may be your next superstar scientists,” Del Pilar said. “You’re limiting a talented group of individuals from achieving all the things they could do not only to uplift their communities but to uplift society.”

title: What One Year of ‘The Public Scholar’ Taught Me
summary:
What One Year of ‘The Public Scholar’ Taught Me
Sara Brady Wed, 09/02/2026 - 03:00 AM

A year of conversations with editors, agents and scholars taught me that breaking through takes practical know-how and remembering how to teach.

Byline(s)
Susan D’Agostino
full_text:
A year ago, I started this column on the premise that the public wants what scholars know and scholars want to share it, but a gap exists between the two. So I asked op-ed editors, literary agents, book editors and scholars who’ve done this work well about how to close that divide. I thought I’d collect a grab bag of tips, and I did. But I also found that breaking through takes two things, and a lot of advice offers only one.

One half of breaking through concerns practicalities. This is a solvable information problem, as many gatekeepers publish clear pitch guidelines about what an op-ed or book proposal must accomplish. Some promising public scholarship sits unwritten because academics forget to look up how to open the gate.

The other half is less concrete. Historian Heather Cox Richardson, author of the Letters From an American newsletter, suggested that scholars need to remember how to teach an audience that has no obligation to keep listening. The idea resonated for me, as I still test my drafts by summoning my decade of teaching, especially those students who did not tolerate poor exposition or boredom. One former student, Michael, never hesitated to blurt out, “Professor, you’re not making any sense!” Another, Jennifer, who was more reticent, showed on her face how much or little she understood. They wanted to understand and feel wonder, like another student, Suman, who could not conceal his delight the day he worked through a rigorous proof that 1 + 1 = 2. So, before submitting my drafts today, I ask, Would Michael have spoken up? Would Jennifer have looked confused? Would Suman have grinned? Then, I revise accordingly.

A scholar who does not summon their teaching instinct when writing for the public risks producing a technically correct story that few readers finish. One who does not understand the submission process will not hear back from editors. Over a year, this column has argued that those who want to write for the public need both at once. Here’s a recap, organized by what you might need.

Before You Write

We sometimes tell ourselves that someone more credentialed or more eloquent should go first. “Don’t Wait for Permission to Write for the Public” helps set that doubt aside.

And because the work needs fuel, “32 Residencies to Fuel Your Writing Dreams” points to places, many of them free, where scholars can find the time that writing for the public demands.

On Craft, by the Gatekeepers

Two pieces take apart the op-ed itself: “What Makes a Great Op-Ed? A Los Angeles Times Editor Explains” unpacks how opinion editor Philip Gray makes decisions, and “How Op-Eds Play the Long Game of Persuasion” explains how opinion pieces change minds, even in a polarized landscape.

In “What Makes a Great Book Proposal? A Literary Agent Explains,” agent Kayla Lightener lays out what a proposal must accomplish, and “3 University Press Editors, 6 Publishing Questions” gathers candid answers from three editors making decisions about which books reach readers: Daniel Taber-Hewett at Oxford University Press, Diana Gillooly at Princeton University Press and Andrew Kinney at UNC Press.

In “Why I Signed With the Literary Agent Who Didn’t Want My Book,” I discuss my experience working with my agent, Marissa Koors at Curious Minds, who challenged my vision for my manuscript.

On Teaching Instinct, From Public Scholars Themselves

Historian David Perry, in “Don’t Let Trolls Keep You Off the Op-Ed Page,” shares how “drafting an op-ed can feel a lot like teaching an 8:30 a.m. Monday class.” Perry argues that op-eds offer more control than classroom teaching, where a student may share or misrepresent your lessons.

In “How One Scholar Is Fighting for Democracy On and Off Campus,” political scientist Jonathan Becker models civic engagement for his students: “If we take ourselves seriously as educators, and if the link between education and democracy is meaningful, then it is incumbent upon us to act.” Becker has since published an op-ed in The New York Times: “What Does the Trump Administration Have Against the 26th Amendment?”

Scholars across disciplines—economics, literature, law, science and more—model how to direct their teaching skills toward public spaces in “Trump Seeks to Silence Critics. These Scholars Are Pushing Back.” In doing so, they offer nuance on consequential topics in fraught times.

Many of these scholars report that writing for the public rekindles what initially drew them their disciplines.

A Final Word From a Popular Public Scholar

In “Heather Cox Richardson Hears the Public Scholar Music,” the well-known history professor, who reaches more than three million newsletter subscribers, told me that “the conceit of the entire project is that we, as human beings in the world in 2026, are all part of a conversation trying to ascertain what’s happening around us.” That is as good a description of public scholarship as I’ve found.

If you’re somewhere in the two-part process—seeing public scholarship as teaching and learning how to break through—I’d like to hear about it. To stay in the conversation, sign up for the Public Scholar newsletter, sent on the first Monday of each month. You’ll get word of each new article in the column, plus behind-the-scenes writing tips and news of other academics finding their voices in public spaces. Your expertise is hard-won. What might happen if you shared it more widely?

title: Understanding the tech giants' oversized influence in American schools
summary: Big tech companies like Apple and Microsoft use devices, training and conferences for teachers and students to embed in schools. The New York Times' Natasha Singer discusses the impact in Coding Kids.
full_text:
Transcript

TERRY GROSS, HOST:

This is FRESH AIR. I'm Terry Gross. It's back-to-school season, and in many classrooms, digital devices have replaced or supplemented books. Tech giants like Google and Microsoft have tried to get schools to buy their products and have offered tech training to teachers and students in subjects like coding, the use of AI, online safety and basic computer tools. So what are the tech giants getting in return for this investment? And how much are they influencing what and how children and teens are taught in schools?

My guest, Natasha Singer, is a New York Times reporter covering the intersection of technology, business and education. She's written a new book titled "Coding Kids: Big Tech's Battle To Remake Public Schools." She writes that in interviewing more than 100 education and tech industry figures for her book and reviewing hundreds of school, government and corporate documents, quote, "it became clear that a handful of giants have used their money, their might and their mammoth platforms to influence nearly every step of the education supply chain," unquote. Singer was a member of a Times reporting team whose coverage of tech industry privacy violations won a George Polk Award in 2019 and was a finalist for a Pulitzer Prize in national reporting.

Natasha Singer, welcome to FRESH AIR. You describe how tech companies have provided things for schools. Are they donating them, or are the schools buying them?

NATASHA SINGER: So public schools in the United States spend billions of dollars a year buying technology for the classroom, including software, math apps, but also computers for every kid. And so those are purchases, and companies like Google and Microsoft have education divisions that sell technology to schools. Then these companies provide software services. Like, if you're gonna buy a Chromebook for every kid, then you need a system to track where the Chromebooks are, and if you're going to give tests, you're going to have to lock down the computer, so that might cost, like, $12 per kid per year.

So there are services that schools pay for. And then on top of that, the companies provide a lot of services that they don't charge schools for, including if you're a client that uses Google apps for your schools, then, you know, you get Gemini, Google's chatbot. And, you know, the teacher training is often funded by tech companies or even led by tech companies. And there are other things like their digital lessons for kids on how to be proficient with spreadsheets or how to, you know, make PowerPoints, or, you know, how to analyze data or how to code that the companies have funded or have made themselves. And those are often free.

GROSS: How do the companies compete with each other to convince schools or, you know, school boards to buy their products as opposed to their competitors' products?

SINGER: So we already have an entrenched system where school districts refer to themselves as, we're a Google district or we're a Microsoft district or we're an Apple district. And so imagine that if you are a wealthy suburban district that can afford to buy MacBooks for all the middle schoolers and high schoolers and iPads for all the elementary schoolers, and Apple comes with a new thing, you know, it's going to fit with the system you're using, and you're going to want to use maybe the Apple coding lessons.

And if you are a huge district like Chicago Public Schools or Miami-Dade County Public Schools and you are a Google district, and your students all have Chromebooks, or you're a Microsoft district, and Google comes and says, like, you can just start using Gemini with your students - and because you already have all the software and apps that Gemini will be embedded in.

And so part of it is the, like, incumbent advantage in school districts. And then when you see newcomers trying to break into this market, so OpenAI, with its ChatGPT chatbot, is one of the newcomers. We have kids who are reporting that they're being bullied or that they have - getting unwanted sexual advances. And the scale of that is really problematic.

And every time, you know, people are making suggestions to Zuckerberg of hiring more safety engineers or changing features to be off by default, either he or somebody who works for him - you see in these emails - says, no. We're not going to do that.

And so some of the things that the companies are agreeing to do now, like turn off notifications in the middle of the night that could wake kids up, turn off notifications during the school day, turn off the beauty filters, put in age verification in a way that's actually rigorous to prevent kids under 13 from being on the platform, are things that inside Meta, people were asking for for years. And so were parents. And so I think that the news of the settlement is big. The proof is in the pudding, because Meta has also promised to make changes for years that parents feel did not go far enough. I think the way it relates to AI is also, though, in the way the system works because the underlying mechanism of social media, which is that they work like slot machines, right? There's an endless feed. You just pull the lever, you get more videos. You pull the lever, you get more photos. You pull the lever, you see more posts and you get more emoji hearts and things, right? It keeps you hooked with variable rewards. And when you use a chatbot and you're a kid, it's very similar. You're asking the chatbot something, you're getting an answer, it's human-like, it's interesting, it's charming, and then it says at the bottom, like, can I also help you do X, Y and Z, right? There's never an end.

And so I think that parents have very similar worries about AI that they have had with social media. They do not trust tech companies to put in safeguards to protect kids from AI and they do not want their kids to be guinea pigs for untested AI in schools.

GROSS: Do tech leaders talk to you or do they see you as being too critical?

SINGER: Both, I think. For my book, I spoke to Brad Smith, who's the president of Microsoft, and he has been one of the leaders in the tech industry pushing for computer science in schools. And I also spoke to Maggie Johnson, who is the head of Google.org, who is his counterpart at Google in terms of, you know, supporting computer science in schools. And I'm grateful that tech executives talk to me because I think it's really important that we understand how tech companies are thinking about what they're doing in schools. And Brad Smith said, philanthropy in the private sector is doing this work because public schools have failed to do what they were supposed to do. And his view is that public schools should be teaching modern subjects like computer science, and they were not equipped to do it fast enough and the tech industry stepped in to help. And is it better than if schools were able to do this themselves? He said, no, but it's certainly better than nothing. And he said to me, you know, think about where we would be on computer science if the tech industry hadn't stepped up.

GROSS: What's your take on that?

SINGER: Well, I've been having this conversation with him for 10 years, and when we started having it 10 years ago, I said to him, I get that, but when big tech companies put their finger on the scale, it tips education in certain ways that not only favor the tech industry but can obscure equally or more important things. So, for example, schools went hog wild for coding, but what about data science?

Data science is a really important subject that teaches kids to analyze datasets, to make things with data, to think about, you know, how data is manipulated by researchers, by trolls on social media. It teaches you, like, when there's statistics in the news to understand if they're right or not. You can read a science paper and understand if this intervention is statistically significant. Data science is a major subject that kids would really benefit from using. And also, you know, you learn math, you can learn some coding. Yet, we are not pushing for data science in schools, and one of the reasons is that there aren't trillion-dollar companies pushing for data science and there aren't tech billionaires going around saying, if you just learn data science you'll get this amazing career, right? And yet, data science is crucial. And when I talked about it with Brad Smith, he said, yeah, we need to push for all the, you know, new subjects, not just computer science. Except that the tech industry pushed for the thing that benefited them.

GROSS: Natasha Singer, thank you so much. Appreciate you coming on our show.

SINGER: Terry, thank you so much.

GROSS: Natasha Singer covers tech in schools for The New York Times. Her new book is titled "Coding Kids: Big Tech's Battle To Remake Public Schools." We recorded our interview yesterday morning. Today, the New York City board of education announced that AI will be banned in the city's public elementary and middle schools. It's part of a larger new policy that will include limits on digital devices in the city's schools. New York City is the nation's largest school system.

Tomorrow on FRESH AIR, our guest will be Paul Greengrass, the director who put us on board "United 93" and made the Bourne movies. His new film, "The Uprising," stars Andrew Garfield as a farmer who leads an army against the king. I hope you'll join us.

title: LeBron James’ $25.5m foundation faced criticism: Why did Akron’s school spark questions?
summary: LeBron James' foundation is dedicated to empowering youth in Akron by providing crucial education and life skills programs. Recently, the I PROMISE School faced challenges due to unsatisfactory state test outcomes. Yet, amidst the critique, the foundation remains steadfast in its support for students and their families. A new collaboration with Nike introduces swimming lessons, focusing on building confidence and enriching life experiences beyond academics.
full_text:
“I’m just trying to understand why”: LeBron James’ $25.5M foundation faced academic criticism while creating new opportunities for Akron’s youth.( Image via: Anthony Behar/Sipa USA/ AP )

LeBron James’ connection with Akron goes well beyond basketball. His foundation has spent years supporting children in his hometown through education and family programs. But the work has also faced difficult questions. The I PROMISE School came under academic scrutiny after disappointing state test results in 2023. Three years later, the foundation continues to back Akron’s children, with a new Nike partnership giving students another opportunity to learn, grow and build confidence. The latest program adds a different kind of lesson. Instead of focusing only on grades, it puts students in the pool and teaches them a skill that can stay with them for life.

Poor test results put LeBron James’ I PROMISE School under serious scrutiny

The criticism became public in July 2023 after Akron Public Schools reviewed state testing data from the 2022-23 school year. The I PROMISE School, which opened in 2018 with support from the LeBron James Family Foundation, faced questions over the academic progress of its students. The numbers were difficult to ignore. No eighth-grade student at I PROMISE had passed the state math test for three straight years, according to reporting published on August 1, 2023. That result drew concern from Akron school officials, especially because I PROMISE serves students who enter school already behind academically. Akron Public Schools Board President Dr. Derrick Hall questioned the results during a July 24, 2023, board meeting. He acknowledged that the pandemic could have affected student performance, but he also pointed out that other students without the same level of resources were performing better. “I’m just trying to understand why. I think it’s fair to ask that question,” Hall said during the meeting. Hall also expressed disappointment because he had hoped I PROMISE could become a model for other schools in the district. His comments put the focus on a difficult issue for LeBron James’ foundation: providing more resources does not automatically guarantee stronger test results. The foundation did not walk away from the school after the criticism. Instead, it stressed its long-term commitment to the students and their families. “When we started this work to wrap around students through education, we entered this partnership with Akron Public School for the long haul,” the foundation said in a statement released after the test results. It also said the work required “long term commitment, hard work, and a lot of love and care.” That response is important because the foundation’s work has continued well beyond the classroom.

Nike partnership gives Akron students another opportunity

On Sept. 2, 2026, the I PROMISE School highlighted its fourth consecutive summer working with Nike on a swim camp. The program gave students the chance to learn swimming while building confidence. The school said first-time swimmers worked through their fears, while returning swimmers took on leadership roles and helped their peers. The program also involved the Firestone High School swim team and U.S. Sports Camps.

The latest financial records also show the scale of the foundation behind the work. Its 2024 Form 990 listed $25.52 million in total assets and $20.96 million in net assets. The foundation reported $7.53 million in revenue and $11.06 million in expenses that year, with about $9 million going toward program services. So the criticism over I PROMISE’s academic results remains an important part of the foundation’s story. But it is not the whole story. LeBron James’ foundation continues to put resources into Akron’s youth, and the Nike swim program shows how that mission now reaches beyond test scores and into skills, confidence and experiences.

title: UNICEF: 1 in 5 youths targeted by online sexual abuse
summary: A survey of around 21,000 young people by the UN's agency for children has found that online sexual abuse of minors is on the rise.
full_text:
The internet is not a safe place for unsupervised children and young people — by now, that's common knowledge.

Social media platforms are adept at tweaking their algorithms to ensure users of any age remain on their sites. To do that, they often disseminate content that can be dangerous and upsetting for young people.

Studies regularly find a connection between what's known as doomscrolling and a higher risk of psychological problems in the young, including suicidal thoughts. And some of the latest trends in video creation on platforms like TikTok directly endanger the safety of users.

In the United States, Meta, which owns both Instagram and Facebook, recently opted to settle a case against it out of court. A number of US states had claimed that the two platforms harmed children.

Meta agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion (€14.7 billion) to the states involved and to limit teenagers' access to its platforms to just two hours a day. During the night, access will be completely blocked.

A new survey by UNICEF, the UN agency for children, puts the spotlight on another danger that young people constantly face in the digital world: sexual assault, a threat experienced by one in five people between the ages of 12 and 17 over the past year.

What are the key findings?

The UNICEF report, which DW saw in advance of publication, explains how such attacks often happen.

"It often begins without warning," the authors of the study wrote. "Conversation becomes coercion, and coercion becomes entrapment."

The survey found that more than 15 million children had been exposed to unwanted sexual content. An estimated 9 million were pressured into sexual conversations or asked to share sexual images, while some 4 million had sexual images shared without their consent. The report's authors, however, warn that the true scale is likely far higher.

"The report reveals a painful reality," said UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell. "These experiences cause profound emotional and mental distress. Many children suffer in silence, unsure where to turn for help."

Often, the perpetrator of the assault puts pressure on a victim. The victims then feel ashamed and this makes it difficult to tell anybody about what has happened. Of those surveyed, 41% had never told anybody about their assault. Others said they had first confided in friends, siblings or their mothers. Fewer than 1% were reported to authorities.

The stereotype many have of a complete stranger harassing young people online actually only applies in 16% of cases. Most perpetrators — 57% — are already known to their victims. They may be friends, family members or even romantic partners.

In addition, 27% of respondents were not able to identify the people behind the profiles. When perpetrators are known, they include adults but also minors. In many cases, attacks take place in real life as well as online.

The major social media platforms are also the main gateways for this kind of behavior. The UNICEF report says 60% of assaults come primarily from Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram (all of which are owned by Meta), followed by Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube. And 14% of respondents cited online gaming platforms as the location of an assault — gaming platforms usually have direct messaging channels.

How was the data collected?

The report polled around 21,000 young people in 21 countries, aged between 12 and 17, who regularly use the internet. Data from 12 countries — Ethiopia, Indonesia, Cambodia, Kenya, Malaysia, Mozambique, Namibia, the Philippines, Tanzania, Thailand, Uganda and Vietnam — had already been collected in 2020 and 2021 and analyzed in an earlier report.

For this new report, additional data was collected in Armenia, Brazil, Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Pakistan and Serbia. The surveys were also supplemented by longer interviews with 100 young people who had experienced abuse.

Europe, US surveys find similar results

Researchers familiar with this issue would not be surprised by the scale of the problem.

The 2020 EU Kids Online Survey, based on a poll conducted in 19 European countries, indicated that 22% of all participants had received sexually explicit messages online.

In a Spanish study conducted in seven secondary schools in 2021 and 2022, 21% of female respondents said they were sexually harassed online "occasionally," while 5% said this happened "frequently." For male respondents in the Spanish study, the percentages were a few points lower.

A similar survey conducted by the Pew Research Center in 2022 found that 17% of 13- to 17-year-olds in the US said they had been sent explicit images without their consent. The survey did not differentiate between sexually explicit content and other material that showed things like violence.

Social media bans in Australia, UK, France

The UNICEF report calls on governments, tech companies and other stakeholders to better protect children and young people in the digital world.

Among the requests:

Design more secure digital platforms, with stronger protection for the privacy of minors.

Strengthen national regulations and criminal law, and close loopholes.

Establish trustworthy reporting and support systems for young people.

Coming just after Meta's out-of-court settlement in the US, the new UNICEF report will likely add fuel to the fire for those seeking to ban social media for young people, an ongoing debate in many countries.

In December 2025, Australia became the first country in the world to introduce an age limit for social media in order to protect minors. There, anyone under 16 is prohibited from having an account on platforms like YouTube, X, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat, a rule the platforms themselves are required to monitor.

A similar age limit will come into effect in the UK in 2027, while France is the first EU country to have passed a law adopting an age limit — 15 years old — for social media users. However, it has since been blocked by France's top court, the Constitutional Council, which ruled it might infringe on freedom of expression and privacy.

In June, a German commission proposed a tiered model. This would come with age limits, requirements for proof of age and strict rules requiring the cooperation of social media platforms.

This article was originally written in German.

title: Wachsamkeit & Verifikation: Wege aus der digitalen Vertrauenskrise
summary:
Es ist eine traurige Wahrheit: Im Internet wie im analogen Leben, im Hochschulbereich wie darüber hinaus, meinen es nicht alle gut mit einem. Deshalb ist es wichtig zu wissen, wie man Falschinformationen erkennt und mit Täuschungen umgeht. In ihrem neuen Blogbeitrag klären Christoph Koitka-Fieke und Simon Vonlanthen über die gängigsten Gefahren in diesem Bereich auf und geben konkrete Ratschläge, wie man sich sicher im Internet und im Hochschulbereich bewegt.

The post Wachsamkeit & Verifikation: Wege aus der digitalen Vertrauenskrise appeared first on Hochschulforum Digitalisierung.
full_text:
Wachsamkeit & Verifikation: Wege aus der digitalen Vertrauenskrise

Wachsamkeit & Verifikation: Wege aus der digitalen Vertrauenskrise

Christoph Koitka-Fieke

Hochschulrektorenkonferenz, Referent für IT & Technologie

Simon Vonlanthen

Es ist eine traurige Wahrheit: Im Internet wie im analogen Leben, im Hochschulbereich wie darüber hinaus meinen es nicht alle gut mit einem. Deshalb ist es wichtig zu wissen, wie man Falschinformationen erkennt und mit Täuschungen umgeht. In ihrem neuen Blogbeitrag klären Christoph Koitka-Fieke und Simon Vonlanthen über die gängigsten Gefahren in diesem Bereich auf und geben konkrete Ratschläge, wie Sie sich sicher im Internet und im Hochschulbereich bewegen. Weiterführende Informationen finden sich in einer Publikation zum selben Thema.

Die maßgebliche Währung von Wissenschaft und Hochschulen ist das Vertrauen: in saubere Arbeit, in belastbare Ergebnisse und in gut informierte Diskursräume. Dieses Vertrauen ist keine Selbstverständlichkeit, sondern wird durch kontinuierliche Bemühungen immer wieder aufgebaut und erhalten.

Genauso gibt es seit jeher Angriffe auf die Integrität von Hochschule und Wissenschaft. Die Digitalisierung hat diese, wie viele andere Felder auch, dynamisiert und vorangetrieben. Es ist heute leichter, Quellen zu fälschen oder Belege zu fabrizieren, als es das noch vor wenigen Jahren der Fall war.

Die Hochschulen sind deswegen diesen Angriffen aber nicht schutzlos ausgeliefert. Die Antworten halten in den meisten Fällen technisch mit. Es geht aber nicht darum, in ein digitales Wettrüsten zwischen falschen und wahren Informationen einzutreten – die Verifikation ist nur eine Säule unseres Ansatzes.

Im Folgenden stellen wir die häufigsten Probleme vor, die im Zusammenhang mit falschen Informationen das Hochschulsystem belasten – und zeigen, wie man ihnen auf individueller Ebene effektiv begegnet.

Fake News

Falschinformationen und gezielte Desinformation stellen Hochschulen vor eine doppelte Herausforderung: Studierende müssen lernen, manipulative Inhalte in sozialen Medien und Nachrichtenquellen zu erkennen. Gleichzeitig sind Hochschulen selbst Ziel von Desinformationskampagnen.

Wenn wissenschaftliche Erkenntnisse (etwa zu Klimawandel, Impfungen oder Pandemien) gezielt verzerrt oder aus dem Kontext gerissen werden, müssen Wissenschaft und Hochschulen sich effektiv wehren können. Medienkompetenz und kritischer Umgang mit Quellen sind schon immer Kernkompetenzen akademischer Bildung – und bleiben auch digital wichtig.

Im deutschsprachigen Raum ist der correctiv-Faktencheck der Goldstandard – hier können auch Beiträge eingeschickt werden.

Das Recherche-Kollektiv Bellingcat ist auf Recherche mit modernen Technologien und öffentlich zugänglichen Daten spezialisiert. Auf der Website wird anhand von echten Recherchen detailliert gezeigt, wie sich Fake News entlarven lassen.

Für den Hochschulkontext ist besonders interessant, in welchen Dimensionen und Konstellationen sich Desinformationen bewegen. Die seit März 2026 geförderten Projekte des BMFTR zum Thema Desinformation – erkennen, verstehen, abwehren zeigen den aktuellen Stand von Forschung. Technik und gesellschaftlicher Debatte.

Deep Fakes und andere KI-Inhalte

KI-generierte Text-, Bild-, Audio- und Videofälschungen eröffnen im Hochschulkontext neue Missbrauchsszenarien: von gefälschten Aussagen prominenter Wissenschaftler:innen über manipulierte Prüfungsvideos bis hin zu gezielter Rufschädigung von Lehrenden oder Studierenden. Besonders problematisch ist die zunehmend niedrige technische und soziale Hemmschwelle bei der Erstellung solcher Inhalte.

Professionelle Kenntnisse oder schwer zugängliche Software sind kaum noch erforderlich. Hochschulen brauchen sowohl technische Detektionswerkzeuge als auch klare Richtlinien und Sanktionsmechanismen, um dieser Bedrohung institutionell begegnen zu können. Für Einzelpersonen ist vor allem wichtig, die Problematik zu kennen und zu wissen, wie man im Zweifel eine Überprüfung durchführt.

Nicht verteufeln – verstehen, Rahmen setzen, Verstöße ahnden – das gilt für Hochschulen als Institution ebenso wie für Lehrende im Hochschulbetrieb.

Prüfen, was echt ist: Der von der EU gefördert „Fake News Debunker“ hilft dabei mit KI-Unterstützung.

Selbst prüfen: Wer weiß, worauf zu achten ist, kann Fake News und Deep Fakes auch ohne technische Hilfe oft schnell erkennen. Mit dieser Checkliste weiß jede:r, worauf zu achten ist.

Predatory Journals

Raubverlage, die gegen Gebühr wissenschaftliche Artikel ohne echte Qualitätssicherung publizieren, untergraben die Integrität des wissenschaftlichen Publikationssystems. Für Nachwuchswissenschaftler:innen, die unter Publikationsdruck stehen, sind sie besonders gefährlich: Wer unwissentlich in einem Predatory Journal veröffentlicht, riskiert nicht nur seinen Ruf, sondern trägt auch zur Verbreitung nicht peer-reviewter und potenziell fehlerhafter Forschungsergebnisse bei. Hochschulen sind gefordert, Forschende frühzeitig über Erkennungsmerkmale unseriöser Verlage aufzuklären und verlässliche Orientierung zu geben.

Das Ombudsgremium für die wissenschaftliche Integrität in Deutschland hat eine detaillierte Handreichung zu Predatory Journals veröffentlicht, die als Orientierung hilfreich ist.

Das Directory of Open Access Journals listet qualitätsgeprüfte Open-Access-Zeitschriften mit Peer Review. Um gelistet zu werden, müssen Zeitschriften ein aufwendiges Bewerbungsverfahren durchlaufen.

Think, Check, Submit ist ein praktisches Online-Tool im Stil einer Checkliste, mit der Forschende testen können, ob der Verlag, der ihre Beiträge veröffentlichen will, seriös und wissenschaftlich ist.

KI-halluzinierte Quellen

Texte, die durch generative KI erstellt werden, können fiktive Quellen beinhalten, die von der KI „halluziniert“ wurden. Dabei können einzelne bibliographische Details halluziniert sein – oder auch die gesamte Quelle. Dies betrifft aber nicht nur Bibliografie-Einträge, sondern kann auch Zitate oder sogar Scans beinhalten. Dies macht die Verifikation von Quellen umso dringlicher.

Zum Glück kann man in vielen Fällen mit wenigen Schritten überprüfen, ob eine Quelle echt ist oder nicht. Das allgemeine Ziel ist es, sie im Netz aufzufinden und dadurch alle ihre Details überprüfen zu können – Autorennamen, Erscheinungsjahr, Titel, Journal/Verlag, Erscheinungsort und gegebenenfalls sogar den konkreten Inhalt. Die folgenden Tools helfen dabei:

Easy-Checks: Angegebene bibliografische Daten lassen sich meistens schnell übers Internet überprüfen. Nebst dem Aufsuchen der Quelle über Suchmaschinen – wir empfehlen DuckDuckGo wegen seiner Privatsphäreneinstellungen – können einzelne Details gezielt überprüft werden:

DOI: Die Homepage der DOI Foundation hat eine Suchmaschine, mit der alle Publikationen mit DOIs („digital object identifier“ – persistente ID für Publikationen) gefunden werden können.

ORCID: Die persistente ID für Forscher:innen kann ebenfalls über eine Search Engine auf der Homepage der vergebenden Organisation gesucht werden.

Datenbanken: Je nach Quelle kann sich die Recherche mittels Suchmaschinen mühsam gestalten. In Publikationsdatenbanken kann teilweise zielgerichteter gesucht werden. Die größten sind Google Scholar und Semantic Scholar. Es gibt aber auch fachspezifische Datenbanken, wie PubMed für Medizin.

Preprints und Zitatsuche: Bei der Verifikation von Zitaten oder größeren Abschnitten ist es ideal, Zugriff auf den Volltext zu haben. Häufig steht dieser aber hinter einer Paywall. Als Gegenmaßnahme kann man einerseits das Zitat oder den Abschnitt auf Suchmaschinen als Ganzes suchen, wodurch man manchmal auf Leseproben verlinkt wird, die die Verifikation des Zitats erlauben. Andererseits helfen auch sog. Preprints. Obschon sie von der publizierten Version abweichen können, sind sie häufig zu weiten Teilen identisch. arXiv ist die größte Datenbank für Preprints, es gibt aber auch fachspezifische Versionen (bspw. bioRxiv für Life Sciences).

Retracted Papers

Im Unterschied zu den Fällen von halluzinierten Quellen oder Deep Fakes sind zurückgezogene Studien („retracted papers“) zwar echt, wurden aber nach ihrer Publikation wieder zurückgezogen. Dies kann aus diversen Gründen geschehen, von unbeabsichtigter Verletzung von Urheberrechten bei einzelnen Grafiken über manipulierte Peer-Reviews bis hin zur Verwendung von anderen zurückgezogenen Studien als Quelle. Bei Studien gilt es also zweierlei zu berücksichtigen: zu überprüfen, ob sie zurückgezogen wurde und wenn ja, weshalb.

Für den Umgang mit den Aussagen einer zurückgezogenen Studie ist entscheidend, ob sie wegen einer Urheberrechtsverletzung zurückgezogen wurde oder ob ihr Design schlecht war. Je nach Grund kann im entsprechenden Journal, bei den Autor:innen oder bei Zitierungen der Quelle durch andere Publikation weiterverfolgt werden, ob und inwiefern die Aussagen dennoch stichhaltig waren.

Um zu überprüfen, ob eine Studie zurückgezogen wurde, findet man häufig auf den Webseiten der Herausgeber einen entsprechenden Vermerk. Achtung: Dieser kann manchmal etwas versteckt sein, solche Webseiten müssen sorgfältig studiert werden.

Die Retraction Watchist die größte Datenbank, die sich auf zurückgezogene Studien spezialisiert hat. Dort wird auch immer gleich der Grund für das Zurückziehen genannt.

Es gibt auch Online-Foren, die sich auf das Post-Publication Peer-Review spezialisiert haben. Dort kann selbst nach genuiner Publikation nachgeschaut werden, ob die Studie gut designt war oder etwaige Mängel aus Sicht der Community aufweist. Ein klassisches Beispiel wäre PubPeer.

Social Engineering

Zur Abrundung der bisher vorgestellten Themen wenden wir uns noch dem Schnittgebiet zwischen Desinformation und Cybersicherheit zu – letzteres ebenfalls ein Aspekt von digitaler Resilienz. Hierzu rückt der „Faktor Mensch“ in den Fokus: Obschon Cybersicherheit eine zentrale Aufgabe der Hochschulverwaltung und -leitung ist, ist es gerade die „Schwachstelle“ des Individuums, die von entscheidender Bedeutung für die Cybersicherheit auf dem Campus ist.

Angreifer verschaffen sich nicht selten über sogenanntes „Social Engineering“ Zugänge zu internen Netzwerken und sensiblen Daten. Dabei ist Social Engineering nichts anderes als das Verwenden von Desinformation zur Täuschung mit den oben genannten Zielen. Die häufigste Form ist dabei das „Phishing“, also das Fischen nach Passwörtern und Zugangsdaten mittels vorgetäuschter Identität über E-Mail, SMS oder Telefon.

Phishing und verwandte Formen sind aber erst notwendig, wenn die Basics der Cybersicherheit funktionieren. Dazu gehört korrektes Passwort-Management sowie Grundvorsicht in der Benutzung des Internets, Social Media, E-Mail und auch künstlicher Intelligenz.

Reguläres Phishing ist meistens weder personen- noch gruppenspezifisch und fällt nicht selten durch gängige Muster auf: schlechte Sprache, Druckmache zu bestimmten Handlungen, obskure Absender-Adressen oder fragwürdige Anhänge. Im Zweifelsfalle hilft es, die Kontaktaufnahme auf unabhängigem Wege zu verifizieren, wie bspw. das BSI vorschlägt.

Beim „Spear-Phishing“ wird vorher gezielt nach Personen oder Gruppen recherchiert, um die Täuschung möglichst gut zu tarnen. Hier gilt: desto weniger man über sich öffentlich preisgibt, desto weniger können Recherchen in öffentlichen Quellen Cyberkriminellen beim (Spear-)Phishing helfen.

Schlussbemerkungen & Fazit

Auf den ersten Blick mögen all diese Tipps und Methoden in ihrer Anzahl und Tiefe überwältigend wirken. An dieser Stelle ist es daher wichtig zu betonen, dass man selbstverständlich nicht jeden News-Artikel, jedes Bild auf den sozialen Medien oder jede wissenschaftliche Publikation ins Detail auf Echtheit überprüfen kann.

Vielmehr gilt es, einen pragmatischen Umgang mit solchen Tools zu entwickeln. Ihr Einsatz ist stark vom Kontext abhängig und muss sich auch lohnen, muss also meist nicht der Standard sein. Eine Methode, um hierzu einen Erfahrungswert aufzubauen, ist es, sich mit folgenden zwei Aspekten zu beschäftigen:

Täuscherperspektive einnehmen: Zu was lohnt es sich überhaupt, zu täuschen? Wenn man eine Gruppe zum Thema X täuschen wollte, wie würde man es tun?

Selbstreflexion: Zu was könnte man mich besonders gut täuschen, weil ich bspw. stark emotional darauf reagiere? Welche persönlichen Schwächen würden dazu ausgenutzt werden?

Wachsamkeit & Verifikation: Wege aus der digitalen Vertrauenskrise

Christoph Koitka-Fieke

Hochschulrektorenkonferenz, Referent für IT & Technologie

Simon Vonlanthen

Es ist eine traurige Wahrheit: Im Internet wie im analogen Leben, im Hochschulbereich wie darüber hinaus meinen es nicht alle gut mit einem. Deshalb ist es wichtig zu wissen, wie man Falschinformationen erkennt und mit Täuschungen umgeht. In ihrem neuen Blogbeitrag klären Christoph Koitka-Fieke und Simon Vonlanthen über die gängigsten Gefahren in diesem Bereich auf und geben konkrete Ratschläge, wie Sie sich sicher im Internet und im Hochschulbereich bewegen. Weiterführende Informationen finden sich in einer Publikation zum selben Thema.

Die maßgebliche Währung von Wissenschaft und Hochschulen ist das Vertrauen: in saubere Arbeit, in belastbare Ergebnisse und in gut informierte Diskursräume. Dieses Vertrauen ist keine Selbstverständlichkeit, sondern wird durch kontinuierliche Bemühungen immer wieder aufgebaut und erhalten.

Genauso gibt es seit jeher Angriffe auf die Integrität von Hochschule und Wissenschaft. Die Digitalisierung hat diese, wie viele andere Felder auch, dynamisiert und vorangetrieben. Es ist heute leichter, Quellen zu fälschen oder Belege zu fabrizieren, als es das noch vor wenigen Jahren der Fall war.

Die Hochschulen sind deswegen diesen Angriffen aber nicht schutzlos ausgeliefert. Die Antworten halten in den meisten Fällen technisch mit. Es geht aber nicht darum, in ein digitales Wettrüsten zwischen falschen und wahren Informationen einzutreten – die Verifikation ist nur eine Säule unseres Ansatzes.

Im Folgenden stellen wir die häufigsten Probleme vor, die im Zusammenhang mit falschen Informationen das Hochschulsystem belasten – und zeigen, wie man ihnen auf individueller Ebene effektiv begegnet.

Fake News

Falschinformationen und gezielte Desinformation stellen Hochschulen vor eine doppelte Herausforderung: Studierende müssen lernen, manipulative Inhalte in sozialen Medien und Nachrichtenquellen zu erkennen. Gleichzeitig sind Hochschulen selbst Ziel von Desinformationskampagnen.

Wenn wissenschaftliche Erkenntnisse (etwa zu Klimawandel, Impfungen oder Pandemien) gezielt verzerrt oder aus dem Kontext gerissen werden, müssen Wissenschaft und Hochschulen sich effektiv wehren können. Medienkompetenz und kritischer Umgang mit Quellen sind schon immer Kernkompetenzen akademischer Bildung – und bleiben auch digital wichtig.

Im deutschsprachigen Raum ist der correctiv-Faktencheck der Goldstandard – hier können auch Beiträge eingeschickt werden.

Das Recherche-Kollektiv Bellingcat ist auf Recherche mit modernen Technologien und öffentlich zugänglichen Daten spezialisiert. Auf der Website wird anhand von echten Recherchen detailliert gezeigt, wie sich Fake News entlarven lassen.

Für den Hochschulkontext ist besonders interessant, in welchen Dimensionen und Konstellationen sich Desinformationen bewegen. Die seit März 2026 geförderten Projekte des BMFTR zum Thema Desinformation – erkennen, verstehen, abwehren zeigen den aktuellen Stand von Forschung. Technik und gesellschaftlicher Debatte.

Deep Fakes und andere KI-Inhalte

KI-generierte Text-, Bild-, Audio- und Videofälschungen eröffnen im Hochschulkontext neue Missbrauchsszenarien: von gefälschten Aussagen prominenter Wissenschaftler:innen über manipulierte Prüfungsvideos bis hin zu gezielter Rufschädigung von Lehrenden oder Studierenden. Besonders problematisch ist die zunehmend niedrige technische und soziale Hemmschwelle bei der Erstellung solcher Inhalte.

Professionelle Kenntnisse oder schwer zugängliche Software sind kaum noch erforderlich. Hochschulen brauchen sowohl technische Detektionswerkzeuge als auch klare Richtlinien und Sanktionsmechanismen, um dieser Bedrohung institutionell begegnen zu können. Für Einzelpersonen ist vor allem wichtig, die Problematik zu kennen und zu wissen, wie man im Zweifel eine Überprüfung durchführt.

Nicht verteufeln – verstehen, Rahmen setzen, Verstöße ahnden – das gilt für Hochschulen als Institution ebenso wie für Lehrende im Hochschulbetrieb.

Prüfen, was echt ist: Der von der EU gefördert „Fake News Debunker“ hilft dabei mit KI-Unterstützung.

Selbst prüfen: Wer weiß, worauf zu achten ist, kann Fake News und Deep Fakes auch ohne technische Hilfe oft schnell erkennen. Mit dieser Checkliste weiß jede:r, worauf zu achten ist.

Predatory Journals

Raubverlage, die gegen Gebühr wissenschaftliche Artikel ohne echte Qualitätssicherung publizieren, untergraben die Integrität des wissenschaftlichen Publikationssystems. Für Nachwuchswissenschaftler:innen, die unter Publikationsdruck stehen, sind sie besonders gefährlich: Wer unwissentlich in einem Predatory Journal veröffentlicht, riskiert nicht nur seinen Ruf, sondern trägt auch zur Verbreitung nicht peer-reviewter und potenziell fehlerhafter Forschungsergebnisse bei. Hochschulen sind gefordert, Forschende frühzeitig über Erkennungsmerkmale unseriöser Verlage aufzuklären und verlässliche Orientierung zu geben.

Das Ombudsgremium für die wissenschaftliche Integrität in Deutschland hat eine detaillierte Handreichung zu Predatory Journals veröffentlicht, die als Orientierung hilfreich ist.

Das Directory of Open Access Journals listet qualitätsgeprüfte Open-Access-Zeitschriften mit Peer Review. Um gelistet zu werden, müssen Zeitschriften ein aufwendiges Bewerbungsverfahren durchlaufen.

Think, Check, Submit ist ein praktisches Online-Tool im Stil einer Checkliste, mit der Forschende testen können, ob der Verlag, der ihre Beiträge veröffentlichen will, seriös und wissenschaftlich ist.

KI-halluzinierte Quellen

Texte, die durch generative KI erstellt werden, können fiktive Quellen beinhalten, die von der KI „halluziniert“ wurden. Dabei können einzelne bibliographische Details halluziniert sein – oder auch die gesamte Quelle. Dies betrifft aber nicht nur Bibliografie-Einträge, sondern kann auch Zitate oder sogar Scans beinhalten. Dies macht die Verifikation von Quellen umso dringlicher.

Zum Glück kann man in vielen Fällen mit wenigen Schritten überprüfen, ob eine Quelle echt ist oder nicht. Das allgemeine Ziel ist es, sie im Netz aufzufinden und dadurch alle ihre Details überprüfen zu können – Autorennamen, Erscheinungsjahr, Titel, Journal/Verlag, Erscheinungsort und gegebenenfalls sogar den konkreten Inhalt. Obschon sie von der publizierten Version abweichen können, sind sie häufig zu weiten Teilen identisch. arXiv ist die größte Datenbank für Preprints, es gibt aber auch fachspezifische Versionen (bspw. bioRxiv für Life Sciences).

Retracted Papers

Im Unterschied zu den Fällen von halluzinierten Quellen oder Deep Fakes sind zurückgezogene Studien („retracted papers“) zwar echt, wurden aber nach ihrer Publikation wieder zurückgezogen. Dies kann aus diversen Gründen geschehen, von unbeabsichtigter Verletzung von Urheberrechten bei einzelnen Grafiken über manipulierte Peer-Reviews bis hin zur Verwendung von anderen zurückgezogenen Studien als Quelle. Bei Studien gilt es also zweierlei zu berücksichtigen: zu überprüfen, ob sie zurückgezogen wurde und wenn ja, weshalb.

Für den Umgang mit den Aussagen einer zurückgezogenen Studie ist entscheidend, ob sie wegen einer Urheberrechtsverletzung zurückgezogen wurde oder ob ihr Design schlecht war. Je nach Grund kann im entsprechenden Journal, bei den Autor:innen oder bei Zitierungen der Quelle durch andere Publikation weiterverfolgt werden, ob und inwiefern die Aussagen dennoch stichhaltig waren.

Um zu überprüfen, ob eine Studie zurückgezogen wurde, findet man häufig auf den Webseiten der Herausgeber einen entsprechenden Vermerk. Achtung: Dieser kann manchmal etwas versteckt sein, solche Webseiten müssen sorgfältig studiert werden.

Die Retraction Watchist die größte Datenbank, die sich auf zurückgezogene Studien spezialisiert hat. Dort wird auch immer gleich der Grund für das Zurückziehen genannt.

Es gibt auch Online-Foren, die sich auf das Post-Publication Peer-Review spezialisiert haben. Dort kann selbst nach genuiner Publikation nachgeschaut werden, ob die Studie gut designt war oder etwaige Mängel aus Sicht der Community aufweist. Ein klassisches Beispiel wäre PubPeer.

Social Engineering

Zur Abrundung der bisher vorgestellten Themen wenden wir uns noch dem Schnittgebiet zwischen Desinformation und Cybersicherheit zu – letzteres ebenfalls ein Aspekt von digitaler Resilienz. Hierzu rückt der „Faktor Mensch“ in den Fokus: Obschon Cybersicherheit eine zentrale Aufgabe der Hochschulverwaltung und -leitung ist, ist es gerade die „Schwachstelle“ des Individuums, die von entscheidender Bedeutung für die Cybersicherheit auf dem Campus ist.

Angreifer verschaffen sich nicht selten über sogenanntes „Social Engineering“ Zugänge zu internen Netzwerken und sensiblen Daten. Dabei ist Social Engineering nichts anderes als das Verwenden von Desinformation zur Täuschung mit den oben genannten Zielen. Die häufigste Form ist dabei das „Phishing“, also das Fischen nach Passwörtern und Zugangsdaten mittels vorgetäuschter Identität über E-Mail, SMS oder Telefon.

Phishing und verwandte Formen sind aber erst notwendig, wenn die Basics der Cybersicherheit funktionieren. Dazu gehört korrektes Passwort-Management sowie Grundvorsicht in der Benutzung des Internets, Social Media, E-Mail und auch künstlicher Intelligenz.

Reguläres Phishing ist meistens weder personen- noch gruppenspezifisch und fällt nicht selten durch gängige Muster auf: schlechte Sprache, Druckmache zu bestimmten Handlungen, obskure Absender-Adressen oder fragwürdige Anhänge. Im Zweifelsfalle hilft es, die Kontaktaufnahme auf unabhängigem Wege zu verifizieren, wie bspw. das BSI vorschlägt.

Beim „Spear-Phishing“ wird vorher gezielt nach Personen oder Gruppen recherchiert, um die Täuschung möglichst gut zu tarnen. Hier gilt: desto weniger man über sich öffentlich preisgibt, desto weniger können Recherchen in öffentlichen Quellen Cyberkriminellen beim (Spear-)Phishing helfen.

Schlussbemerkungen & Fazit

Auf den ersten Blick mögen all diese Tipps und Methoden in ihrer Anzahl und Tiefe überwältigend wirken. An dieser Stelle ist es daher wichtig zu betonen, dass man selbstverständlich nicht jeden News-Artikel, jedes Bild auf den sozialen Medien oder jede wissenschaftliche Publikation ins Detail auf Echtheit überprüfen kann.

Vielmehr gilt es, einen pragmatischen Umgang mit solchen Tools zu entwickeln. Ihr Einsatz ist stark vom Kontext abhängig und muss sich auch lohnen, muss also meist nicht der Standard sein.
